notes.h: Planning meals with the current dietary guidelines
notes.b: Ireland's national guide to healthy eating is the Department of Health healthy eating guidelines and the Healthy Eating Food Pyramid, published under Healthy Ireland. A balanced diet follows the pyramid, so it contains all the nutrients in the correct proportions.
points: Vegetables, salad and fruit, together with wholemeal cereals, breads, potatoes, pasta and rice, make up the foundation shelves of the pyramid, so these are the foods eaten most often.
Fruit and vegetables: five or more servings a day are recommended, and up to seven, because they supply vitamins, minerals and fibre.
Milk, yoghurt and cheese, preferably the lower-fat versions, supply calcium and protein; three servings a day are given in menu answers.
Meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans, pulses and nuts supply protein; two servings a day, and at least two portions of fish a week are advised, one of them oily fish.
Fats, spreads and oils sit on a small shelf and are used in small amounts, with unsaturated oils preferred to saturated fat.

The top shelf holds foods and drinks high in fat, sugar and salt. They are not needed for health, so they are limited to once or twice a week at most; sugary drinks are limited too, and water is the main drink.
Salt intake is kept low by cooking with less salt and reading labels, and portion sizes are controlled so that energy intake is balanced with activity.
When planning, choose wholegrain, lean meat and lower-fat dairy, vary the foods eaten, and use less salt and sugar.
notes.tip: If you are asked to comment on a day's meals, judge them against the pyramid: name the strengths and weaknesses, then suggest improvements. Do not claim that starchy foods sit at the base; say that vegetables, salad and fruit and the wholemeal cereals group form the foundation shelves.

notes.b: Good planning starts with who is being fed and ends with a plan for cooking. Meals are then chosen so that the whole day, not just one meal, matches the pyramid.
points: Planning begins with the people being fed: their ages, health needs, activity, likes and dislikes, any special diets, and the number to feed.
Each meal includes a starchy food, fruit or vegetables, and a protein food or dairy, so that all the pyramid groups are covered across the day.
Breakfast is not skipped, because it supplies energy for the morning, and a packed lunch or snack supplies fruit and wholegrain foods between meals.
Colour, flavour, texture and cooking method are varied, and the same food is not repeated in a day, so that meals are appetising and not repetitive.
Portion sizes are matched to age, appetite and activity, and energy is balanced across the day.
A three-meal menu sets out breakfast, lunch and dinner, often with a drink or snack. Name actual dishes, then show how they meet the person's needs.

The steps in planning are: 1. decide the menus for the week. 2. Check the food and equipment already at home. 3. Write a shopping list. 4. Buy the food. 5. Schedule the cooking order and timing, after checking cooking time, budget and equipment.
When a question names a person such as a pregnant woman, teenager, vegetarian, coeliac or person with CHD (coronary heart disease), apply that group's requirements to the menu.
notes.tip: Set the menu out as named dishes and drinks, never as a list of food groups, then add a brief reason linked to the person. The menu must suit them: a pregnant woman cannot have pâté or raw egg, a coeliac cannot have wheat, and a lacto-vegetarian eats no meat, fish or eggs.

notes.b: The cook's own ability decides which meals are realistic. Skill affects both what can be made and how consistent the results are.
points: A skilled cook can adapt recipes, for example to add fibre, reduce fat or cater for a special diet, and can make dishes from raw ingredients.
A less experienced cook may rely on convenience foods, so simple recipes with few stages suit them.
Following a tested recipe with accurate measures gives consistent results and portion sizes.
Nutrition knowledge, such as reading labels and knowing the guidelines, helps a cook choose healthy meals, and skills can be built by cooking with others.
notes.tip: When asked how money, time and equipment affect family meal planning, give each resource its own point with a clear effect on what is cooked.

notes.b: Time available on the day decides how elaborate a meal can be. Planning ahead lets a busy household still eat well.
points: Dishes are chosen to suit the time available; quick dishes such as stir-fries, omelettes, soups and grills suit a limited preparation time.
Batch cooking large quantities and freezing portions saves time on later days, because a meal is ready after reheating.
Time can also be saved by preparing ahead, using convenience foods sensibly, and cooking one meal in stages.
For families with irregular routines, keep a shopping list and staple stocks, and use bulk buying and special offers sensibly.

For irregular routines, also keep some prepared or frozen ingredients and reheatable, freezable batches, use a slow cooker or timer, and pack meals, while keeping the diet balanced and portions sensible.
notes.tip: Questions on families with irregular routines ask for strategies for purchasing and for planning. Give both: for example a list and staple stocks for buying, and frozen batches and a slow cooker for cooking.

notes.b: The equipment in the kitchen decides which cooking methods are possible. The right appliances also save both time and energy.
points: Equipment available decides what can be cooked: oven, hob, grill, microwave, pressure cooker, slow cooker, food processor, blender and freezer. A lack of equipment limits the methods that can be used.
A microwave, pressure cooker, slow cooker or food processor reduces cooking and preparation time; microwave reheating also saves energy.
A freezer permits batch cooking and bulk buying, because portions and large purchases can be stored until needed.
Frozen foods keep their nutritional and sensory quality, and frozen fruit and vegetables are frozen at peak ripeness, retain most of their nutrients and reduce waste.
Frozen foods also save time and money, add variety and out-of-season foods, allow portion control and make emergency meals possible.
Freezers should be kept at -18 °C, and cooked food should not be left between 5 °C and 63 °C, the range in which bacteria multiply quickly.
notes.tip: A question on the benefits of frozen foods in meal planning is looking for several: nutrition and quality, time and money saved, variety, less waste, portion control and emergency meals.

notes.h: Resources: money and choice of foods
notes.b: A limited budget does not have to mean a poor diet if meals are planned before shopping. Low-income families have limited choice, so careful planning matters most for them.
points: Set a budget, plan menus before shopping, and write a shopping list and keep to it. This prevents impulse buying and waste.
Compare prices, including unit prices, and use special offers sensibly. Bulk buying suits only foods that will be used or frozen.
Seasonal produce is usually cheaper and fresher than out-of-season imports.
Own-brand products are often cheaper than branded equivalents; compare labels and unit prices.
Pulses, eggs and tinned fish are inexpensive sources of protein, as are less expensive cuts of meat, and growing food or batch cooking can also cut costs.
Cheap processed foods are often high in salt, sugar and fat, so budget plans should still include fresh produce, wholegrains and milk.
Foods are chosen for nutritive value, cost, availability and season, suitability for the people (age, health), preparation time and storage, and labels and dates are checked.
Food is stored so that it stays safe and usable: in the fridge, freezer or cupboard, with a vegetable drawer for vegetables, and with stock rotation.
notes.tip: For a money question, name the budget and cheaper protein, then add that cheap processed foods can be high in salt, sugar and fat. Keep planning (before), preparation (during cooking) and storage (after) as separate ideas.

notes.h: Reducing food waste and the food bill
notes.b: Food that is thrown away is money wasted. Planning, correct storage and understanding dates on packs all cut waste and the food bill.
points: Plan meals and shop with a list, check what is already at home, and buy only what is needed.
A use-by date relates to food safety and food must not be eaten after it; a best-before date relates to quality, and food may still be safe after it.
Stock is rotated so that older items are used first.
Food is stored correctly, and food that will not be used in time is frozen before its use-by date.
Leftovers are planned into the next day's meals, for example turning a roast into soup or a pie, and the right portions are cooked; scraps can be composted.
Reducing waste saves money and reduces environmental harm, such as landfill and greenhouse gas emissions.
notes.tip: When asked to suggest ways of reducing food waste or the food bill, give separate points on planning and shopping lists, date marks, stock rotation, freezing and using leftovers.

keyTerms.definition: A diagram from the Food Safety Authority of Ireland that shows the foods to eat most often at its base and those to eat sparingly at its top.
The date after which a food should not be eaten, for safety reasons.
The date until which a food keeps its best quality; it may still be safe to eat after this date.
Preparing a large quantity of a dish at one time and storing the portions for later use.
The temperature range of 5 °C to 63 °C in which bacteria multiply rapidly in food.
The price of a product per standard quantity, such as per kilogram, used to compare value between sizes and brands.
Serving food in amounts matched to a person's energy needs and appetite.
Food that is ready to eat or needs little preparation, such as ready meals and pre-cut vegetables.

factCards.term: Three steps when planning a menu
factCards.definition: Consider the people and their needs; check the nutritional balance across the day; check time, cost and equipment before shopping.

factCards.term: Foods at the base of the Irish Food Pyramid
factCards.definition: Wholegrain starchy foods such as bread, cereals, potatoes, pasta and rice, eaten most often.

factCards.term: Three benefits of frozen foods in meal planning
factCards.definition: They retain nutritional and sensory quality; they save time and money; they reduce food waste.

factCards.term: Difference between a use-by and a best-before date
factCards.definition: A use-by date is about safety and food must not be eaten after it; a best-before date is about quality.

factCards.term: Three ways to reduce the food bill
factCards.definition: Use a shopping list; buy seasonal and own-brand foods; plan meals to use leftovers.

factCards.term: Two time-saving appliances for meal preparation
factCards.definition: A microwave oven and a pressure cooker.

factCards.term: Temperature range of the danger zone
factCards.definition: 5 °C to 63 °C, the range in which bacteria multiply quickly.

questions.prompt: Outline three ways in which money available affects family meal planning.
questions.model: Money: a fixed budget limits the range of foods, so a family plans meals around cheaper, nutritious foods such as pulses, eggs and seasonal produce. Shopping: a written list and comparison of unit prices stop impulse buying and waste. Quality: a tight budget may mean choosing own-brand or processed foods, so the planner balances these with fresh fruit, vegetables and wholegrains. Any three ways, each explained, earn 6 marks.

questions.prompt: Plan a day of three meals for a family of four on a limited budget, explaining how the current dietary guidelines, time, equipment and food waste are taken into account.
questions.model: Guidelines: each meal includes a wholegrain starch, fruit or vegetables, and a protein food or dairy, with fish at least twice a week, one of them oily. Breakfast: porridge made with milk and topped with fruit, and wholemeal toast. Lunch: homemade vegetable and lentil soup with wholemeal bread, followed by a yoghurt and an apple. Dinner: a bean and vegetable chilli made in a slow cooker with brown rice and a side of seasonal vegetables. Budget: a shopping list, own-brand and seasonal produce, and pulses as the main protein. Time and equipment: the soup and chilli are made in batches and portions are frozen; the slow cooker frees time during the day. Waste: leftovers are used for the next day's lunch and food is frozen before its use-by date. Water is the main drink.
